frozen_original.title: ICE Conducts Sweeping Raids and Mass Arrests in Major Cities
frozen_original.synopsis: In a coordinated operation in July 2025, ICE agents conducted sweeping raids across several major U.S. cities, resulting in thousands of arrests. The operations targeted neighborhoods and workplaces with little regard for legal status, sweeping up citizens and permanent residents in the chaos. Reports emerged of widespread civil rights violations and excessive force during the detentions.

primary.description_medium: The supplied entry alleges that ICE coordinated raids across major U.S. cities on July 21, 2025, producing thousands of arrests and civil-rights violations. It also alleges that citizens and permanent residents were caught up in the operation. The packet does not identify the operation or corroborate its scope, date, arrests, or excessive-force claims; this draft is not publication-eligible.
primary.description_long: The supplied record alleges that a coordinated ICE operation took place on July 21, 2025, across several major U.S. cities. It says the raids produced thousands of arrests, swept up citizens and permanent residents along with people targeted for immigration enforcement, and involved civil-rights violations and excessive force. These are allegations from the frozen entry, not established findings. The packet names no city, operation, arrest total, person, court case, eyewitness, or contemporaneous report that would let a reader verify the claims. A Guardian data analysis published two days later reported that June average daily ICE arrests were 268% higher than in June 2024 and described separate large-scale Los Angeles raids. That context does not document this specific July 21 operation or confirm the claimed arrests, status of those detained, or use of force. The event's exact date, scope, affected people, and alleged conduct remain unverified. This copy is internal only until source evidence identifies the operation and supports its central claims.

frozen_original.title: Pam Bondi DOJ Drops All Pending Cases Against Trump Allies on Day One
frozen_original.synopsis: On January 20, 2025, within hours of her confirmation as Attorney General, Pam Bondi directed the DOJ to drop all pending federal cases against Trump associates and allies, including cases that had been brought by career prosecutors following the January 6 investigation and other matters. The mass dismissal of cases bypassed normal DOJ review processes and was carried out without explanation of the merits. Career DOJ prosecutors who had worked the cases for years described the action as politically motivated and legally unjustifiable. The move was characterized by former officials as an unprecedented purge of legitimate prosecutions for purely political purposes, effectively ending DOJ independence as a check on presidential power.

primary.title: Pam Bondi DOJ Drops All Pending Cases Against Trump Allies on Day One
blockers: The date and actor in the frozen record conflict with the accessed confirmation report: the Senate confirmed Bondi on February 4, 2025, so she was not Attorney General on January 20 and could not have ordered the claimed action as Attorney General that day.

No accessed source supports the broader allegation that Bondi directed dismissal of all pending federal cases against Trump allies on January 20. The closest documented action is President Trump’s January 20 clemency proclamation, which addressed January 6-related convictions and directed dismissal of pending indictments for conduct related to the Capitol events; it is a different actor and a narrower category than all cases against Trump associates.

The supplied counterpart entry-6611 repeats the day-one Bondi allegation with different case categories. Entry-6788 separately alleges a February motion to vacate all January 6 convictions and explicitly distinguishes it from Trump’s January 20 clemency order. Neither is a confirmed survivor, so this record cannot be converted into a duplicate merge or a second card about the proclamation.

frozen_original.title: Trump Ends Protected Status for Millions of Refugees — TPS Ended for Afghans and Ukrainians
frozen_original.synopsis: In March 2025, the Trump administration terminated Temporary Protected Status designations for hundreds of thousands of Afghans, Ukrainians, Venezuelans, Haitians, Salvadorans, and other nationals who had been granted protection from deportation due to ongoing armed conflict, environmental disasters, or extraordinary dangerous conditions in their home countries. Afghans who had fled Taliban persecution — many with direct ties to U.S. military and diplomatic operations — and Ukrainians who had fled the Russian invasion faced forced return to active war zones. Immigration advocates argued the terminations violated both U.S. and international law obligations not to return individuals to places where they face serious harm. Hundreds of thousands of people who had lived, worked, and paid taxes in the United States for years suddenly faced imminent deportation to countries in active conflict.

primary.title: DHS Ends Afghanistan’s TPS Designation Effective July 14, 2025
primary.description_short: DHS terminated Afghanistan’s Temporary Protected Status designation, effective July 14, 2025.
primary.description_medium: On May 13, 2025, DHS published a notice terminating Afghanistan’s Temporary Protected Status designation, effective July 14. The notice estimates about 11,700 Afghan nationals and people without nationality last resident in Afghanistan held TPS; it separately notes about 3,600 were also approved lawful permanent residents. The sourced action concerns Afghanistan only and does not establish deportations or simultaneous TPS terminations for other nationalities.
primary.description_long: On May 13, 2025, DHS published a notice terminating Afghanistan’s designation for Temporary Protected Status (TPS). The notice says the Secretary reviewed country conditions, consulted other U.S. agencies, and determined that Afghanistan no longer met the statutory conditions for TPS. The designation ended effective at 11:59 p.m. local time on July 14, 2025. DHS estimated approximately 11,700 Afghan nationals and people without nationality who last habitually resided in Afghanistan held TPS under that designation. The notice also states that approximately 3,600 of that group had already been approved as lawful permanent residents. This entry is narrowed to the Afghanistan designation; it does not claim that Ukraine, Venezuela, Haiti, El Salvador, or other designations ended in the same March action. The notice establishes a change in legal status, not that former TPS holders were deported, returned to danger, or all lacked another immigration status. Those individual outcomes and the legal merits of the Secretary’s assessment are outside the evidence used here.

source_fact_map.source_excerpt: This termination is effective July 14, 2025. After July 14, 2025, nationals of Afghanistan (and aliens having no nationality who last habitually resided in Afghanistan) who have been granted TPS under Afghanistan's designation will no longer have TPS.

corrected_proposal.title: DHS Ends Afghanistan’s TPS Designation Effective July 14, 2025
corrected_proposal.description_short: DHS terminated Afghanistan’s Temporary Protected Status designation, effective July 14, 2025.
corrected_proposal.description_medium: On May 13, 2025, DHS published a notice terminating Afghanistan’s Temporary Protected Status designation, effective July 14. The notice estimates about 11,700 Afghan nationals and people without nationality last resident in Afghanistan held TPS; it separately notes about 3,600 were also approved lawful permanent residents. The sourced action concerns Afghanistan only and does not establish deportations or simultaneous TPS terminations for other nationalities.
corrected_proposal.description_long: On May 13, 2025, DHS published a notice terminating Afghanistan’s designation for Temporary Protected Status (TPS). The notice says the Secretary reviewed country conditions, consulted other U.S. agencies, and determined that Afghanistan no longer met the statutory conditions for TPS. The designation ended effective at 11:59 p.m. local time on July 14, 2025. DHS estimated approximately 11,700 Afghan nationals and people without nationality who last habitually resided in Afghanistan held TPS under that designation. The notice also states that approximately 3,600 of that group had already been approved as lawful permanent residents. This entry is narrowed to the Afghanistan designation; it does not claim that Ukraine, Venezuela, Haiti, El Salvador, or other designations ended in the same March action. The notice establishes a change in legal status, not that former TPS holders were deported, returned to danger, or all lacked another immigration status. Those individual outcomes and the legal merits of the Secretary’s assessment are outside the evidence used here.

frozen_original.synopsis: Trump's crypto company, World Liberty Financial, has been approved as a national bank by a federal regulator headed by a Trump appointee. This has raised concerns about conflicts of interest and the potential for Trump to profit from his presidency.

source_quotes.quote: announced it had received preliminary approval from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) to operate its subsidiary World Liberty Financial Trust as a national trust bank on Aug. 14.
source_quotes.source_excerpt: President Donald Trump’s crypto company received approval to operate a bank from a federal regulator headed by a Trump appointee. World Liberty Financial, the crypto company launched in 2024 by President Donald Trump and his sons Don Jr. and Eric, announced it had received preliminary approval from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) to operate its subsidiary World Liberty Financial Trust as a national trust bank on Aug. 14. The OCC would not comment on a specific charter application, a spokesperson said in an email that the chartering process “is transparent, apolitical and nonpartisan,” and overseen by “seasoned civil servants.”

The OCC hereby grants preliminary conditional approval of your charter application upon determining that your proposal meets certain regulatory and policy requirements. The OCC has granted preliminary conditional approval only. Final approval and authorization pursuant to 12 USC 27(a) for the Bank to commence business will not be granted until all preopening requirements are met.
